courses.title: Geotechnical Engineering · Unit 1 · Soil formation, index properties and classification
courses.summary: Soil formation and types, three-phase diagram and weight–volume relations, specific gravity, density, void ratio, porosity, degree of saturation, relative density, grain-size analysis (sieve and hydrometer), Atterberg limits and indices, and the Indian Standard soil classification system.
outcomes: Use phase relations to compute e, n, S, w and densities
Compute Atterberg indices and read the plasticity chart
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A lab receives a wet soil sample from a building site.
Weighing it wet and dry gives everything needed for phase relations.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
Water content w = W_w/W_s; void ratio e = V_v/V_s; porosity n = V_v/V = e/(1 + e); degree of saturation S = V_w/V_v.
Key relations: Se = wG; γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + e) = γ/(1 + w); γ_sat = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e); γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w; γ_bulk = (G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e).
Air content a_c = V_a/V_v; percentage air voids n_a = n·a_c.
Relative density D_r = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Water content relative to total weight (it's relative to dry solids).
- Using n and e interchangeably.
- Forgetting γ_w = 9.81 kN/m³ (or 10 if the problem says so).

activity.prompt: Saturated soil: w = 30%, G = 2.65. Void ratio e?

quiz.why: The fundamental relation of soil mechanics is S e = w G: degree of saturation × void ratio = water content × specific gravity of solids.
Porosity n = V_v/V and e = V_v/V_s. Since V = V_s(1 + e), n = e/(1 + e).
Dry unit weight γ_d = weight of solids/total volume = Gγ_w/(1 + e).

quiz.q: Water content is defined relative to
quiz.why: Water content is the weight of water divided by the weight of solids (dry weight), not the total weight, so it can exceed 100%.
A relative density of 80% falls in the 65–85% range, which is called dense. Below 15% is very loose, and above 85% very dense.

scenes.text: An earth dam's filter must stop fine soil washing out but still drain.
Grain-size curves tell how well-graded each material is.

steps.title: Tests and coefficients
steps.body:
Sieve analysis for coarse soil (> 75 µm); hydrometer (sedimentation, Stokes' law) for fines.
D₁₀ (effective size), D₃₀, D₆₀ from the curve. Uniformity coefficient C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀; coefficient of curvature C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀D₆₀).
Well-graded gravel: C_u > 4, 1 ≤ C_c ≤ 3; well-graded sand: C_u > 6, 1 ≤ C_c ≤ 3. Uniform (poorly graded) soils have C_u near 1; gap-graded have C_c outside the range.
IS sizes: gravel 80–4.75 mm, sand 4.75–0.075 mm, silt 0.075–0.002 mm, clay < 0.002 mm.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** D₁₀ = 0.15, D₃₀ = 0.40, D₆₀ = 1.2 mm: C_u = 8, C_c = 0.16/0.18 = 0.89 ⇒ C_c < 1 ⇒ poorly graded sand (SP).

**Example 2.** D₁₀ = 0.1, D₃₀ = 0.35, D₆₀ = 0.8: C_u = 8, C_c = 1.53 ⇒ well-graded sand (SW).

**Example 3.** Stokes: particle 0.01 mm, G = 2.7, μ = 0.001 Pa·s: v = (2.7 − 1)(9810)(10⁻⁵)²/(18 × 0.001) = 9.3×10⁻⁵ m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading D₁₀ as the 10th sieve rather than the 10% finer size.
- Applying gravel criteria to sand.
- Hydrometer results without dispersing agent.

activity.prompt: D₁₀ = 0.2 mm, D₆₀ = 1.4 mm. Uniformity coefficient?

quiz.why: The coefficient of uniformity is C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀, which indicates the spread of grain sizes.
A soil is well graded when the coefficient of curvature C_c = D₃₀²/(D₁₀D₆₀) lies between 1 and 3 (and C_u is large enough).
In IS classification sand is 4.75 mm to 0.075 mm. Gravel is larger and silt/clay smaller.
Hydrometer analysis finds the size of fine particles from their settling speed in water, using Stokes' law.
The effective size is D₁₀, the diameter below which 10% of the soil is finer (used in Hazen's formula).

scenes.text: Houses on black cotton soil in central India crack as the soil swells and shrinks.
Atterberg limits predict that behaviour.

steps.title: Limits and indices
steps.body:
Liquid limit w_L (Casagrande cup: 25 blows), plastic limit w_P (3 mm thread crumbles), shrinkage limit w_S.
Plasticity index I_P = w_L − w_P; liquidity index I_L = (w − w_P)/I_P; consistency index I_C = (w_L − w)/I_P = 1 − I_L.
Activity A = I_P/(% clay fraction < 2 µm): inactive < 0.75, normal 0.75–1.25, active > 1.25 (montmorillonite highly active).
Flow index I_f = slope of water content vs log(blows); toughness index I_T = I_P/I_f.
Shrinkage limit (from dry pat): w_S = (V_d/W_d − 1/G)γ_w × 100 (method dependent).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** w_L = 60%, w_P = 25%, w = 40%: I_P = 35; I_L = 0.43; I_C = 0.57 (stiff-ish).

**Example 2.** I_P = 35, clay fraction 25% ⇒ A = 1.4 (active — likely expansive).

**Example 3.** Natural w > w_L ⇒ I_L > 1 ⇒ very soft, may behave like a liquid when disturbed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping liquid and plastic limits.
- Using total fines instead of < 2 µm clay fraction for activity.
- Interpreting negative I_L as an error (it means the soil is drier than the plastic limit — stiff).

activity.prompt: w_L = 48%, w_P = 22%, natural w = 35%. Liquidity index?

quiz.why: Plasticity index I_P = w_L − w_P, the water content range over which the soil is plastic.

quiz.q: Liquid limit cup test standard blows
quiz.why: In the Casagrande cup test the liquid limit is the water content at which the groove closes in 25 blows.
Skempton's activity A = plasticity index/clay fraction (% finer than 2 μm).
Montmorillonite has a weak, water-absorbing structure and is highly expansive. Kaolinite is much less so, and illite is intermediate.
Consistency index I_C = (w_L − w)/I_P and liquidity index I_L = (w − w_P)/I_P. Adding gives (w_L − w_P)/I_P = 1.

scenes.text: A geotechnical report labels a soil 'CH' — highly plastic clay.
IS 1498 uses grain size and the plasticity chart.

steps.title: IS 1498 system
steps.body:
Coarse-grained: > 50% retained on 75 µm. Gravel (G) if > half of coarse fraction retained on 4.75 mm, else sand (S). Suffix W/P (well/poorly graded, if fines < 5%), M/C (silty/clayey fines, if fines > 12%), dual symbols for 5–12%.
Fine-grained: > 50% passes 75 µm. Plasticity chart: A-line I_P = 0.73(w_L − 20). Above A-line ⇒ clay (C); below ⇒ silt (M); organic (O). Compressibility: L (w_L < 35), I (35–50), H (> 50).
Peat (Pt) — highly organic.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 70% passing 75 µm, w_L = 55, I_P = 30: A-line value 0.73 × 35 = 25.6 < 30 ⇒ above ⇒ CH.

**Example 2.** w_L = 40, I_P = 8: A-line 14.6 > 8 ⇒ below ⇒ MI.

**Example 3.** 60% sand, 35% gravel, 5% fines, C_u = 8, C_c = 1.5 ⇒ SW.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 50% instead of the IS boundaries (35/50) for compressibility.
- Forgetting the A-line equation.
- Classifying coarse soils without checking fines percentage.

activity.prompt: Classify (IS 1498)

quiz.why: On the plasticity chart, the A-line is I_P = 0.73(w_L − 20). Soils above it are clays, and those below are silts or organic soils.
A soil is fine-grained when more than 50% passes the 75 μm sieve.
In IS classification, high compressibility (H) means w_L > 50%; intermediate (I) is 35–50% and low (L) is below 35%.

quiz.q: Dual symbols used when fines are
quiz.why: Dual symbols (such as SW-SM) are used when the fines are between 5% and 12%.
Pt is the symbol for peat and other highly organic soils.

questions.why: Void ratio is volume of voids over volume of solids, which can exceed 1, as it commonly does for soft clays and organic soils.
In IS classification, clay-size particles are smaller than 0.002 mm.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A soil with natural water content above its liquid limit has I_L > 1.  Reason (R): I_L = (w − w_P)/(w_L − w_P) exceeds 1 when w > w_L.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: I_L = (w − w_P)/(w_L − w_P) is greater than 1 when w > w_L, so the soil is in a liquid state. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Degree of saturation: w 20%, G 2.7, e 0.72

questions.why: A = I_P/clay fraction = 20/40 = 0.5. Values below 0.75 are inactive.

questions.q: Case: A site soil has w_L 52, I_P 32, 85% fines. IS symbol
questions.why: Fines are more than 50%, and w_L > 50 means high compressibility. The A-line at w_L = 52 is 0.73 × 32 = 23.4. Since I_P = 32 is above it, the soil is a clay, so CH.
Air voids as a fraction of the total volume = n(1 − S) = 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.08 = 8%.

questions.q: Wet mass 1.9 kg, dry 1.6 kg, V 1000 cm³, G 2.7: e

courses.title: Geotechnical Engineering · Unit 2 · Permeability, seepage and effective stress
courses.summary: Darcy's law, permeability tests (constant head, falling head, pumping), factors affecting k, equivalent permeability of layered soils, effective stress principle, seepage pressure and quick sand, flow nets and seepage discharge, and capillarity in soils.
outcomes: Compute k from lab and field tests
Find equivalent permeability of layered deposits
Apply σ′ = σ − u with and without seepage
Use flow nets for seepage and check against piping (quick condition)
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A basement excavation fills with groundwater.
How fast water seeps depends on the soil's permeability k.

steps.title: Darcy and tests
steps.body:
Darcy: v = ki (laminar), q = kiA. Seepage velocity v_s = v/n.
- Constant head (coarse soils): k = QL/(Aht).
- Falling head (fine soils): k = (aL/(At)) ln(h₁/h₂) = 2.303(aL/(At)) log₁₀(h₁/h₂).
- Field pumping (unconfined): k = q ln(r₂/r₁)/(π(h₂² − h₁²)); confined: k = q ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πb(h₂ − h₁)).
Typical k (m/s): gravel 10⁻² +, sand 10⁻³–10⁻⁵, silt 10⁻⁶–10⁻⁸, clay < 10⁻⁹.
Hazen: k (cm/s) ≈ C D₁₀² (D₁₀ in cm, C ≈ 100).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Constant head: Q = 500 cm³ in 100 s, L = 20 cm, A = 50 cm², h = 40 cm: k = 500 × 20/(50 × 40 × 100) = 0.05 cm/s.

**Example 2.** Falling head: a = 1 cm², A = 50 cm², L = 10 cm, h from 100 to 50 cm in 600 s: k = (1 × 10/(50 × 600)) ln 2 = 2.31×10⁻⁴ cm/s.

**Example 3.** Hazen: D₁₀ = 0.2 mm = 0.02 cm ⇒ k ≈ 100 × 0.0004 = 0.04 cm/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln vs log₁₀ without the 2.303 factor.
- Using discharge velocity as the actual velocity (divide by n).
- Applying Darcy's law to turbulent flow in coarse gravels.

activity.prompt: Constant head test: Q = 300 cm³ in 60 s, L = 15 cm, A = 30 cm², h = 25 cm. k (cm/s)?

quiz.why: Darcy's law says discharge velocity is proportional to the hydraulic gradient: v = ki.
The falling head test is used for fine-grained soils, where k is low and flow is too slow for a constant head test.
Seepage velocity is the real water velocity through the pores: v_s = v/n, larger than the discharge velocity.
Clays have very small pores, and their permeability is very low, below about 10⁻⁹ m/s.
Hazen's formula k = C·D₁₀² uses the effective size D₁₀.

lessons.title: Layered soils and factors affecting permeability

scenes.text: A site has sand, clay and silt layers one above another.
Water moves far more easily along the layers than across them.

steps.title: Equivalent permeability
steps.body:
Flow parallel to layers: k_h = Σkᵢ Hᵢ/ΣHᵢ (weighted mean).
Flow perpendicular: k_v = ΣHᵢ/Σ(Hᵢ/kᵢ) (harmonic-type mean).
Always k_h ≥ k_v. Factors: grain size (k ∝ D²), void ratio (k ∝ e³/(1 + e) — Kozeny–Carman), fluid viscosity (temperature), soil structure, degree of saturation, entrapped air.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Layers: 2 m sand (k = 10⁻⁴ m/s), 1 m clay (10⁻⁸), 2 m silt (10⁻⁶).
k_h = (2×10⁻⁴ + 10⁻⁸ + 2×10⁻⁶)/5 = 4.04×10⁻⁵ m/s.
k_v = 5/(2/10⁻⁴ + 1/10⁻⁸ + 2/10⁻⁶) = 5/(2×10⁴ + 10⁸ + 2×10⁶) = 4.9×10⁻⁸ m/s — controlled by the clay.

**Example 2.** Temperature: k₂₀ = k_T μ_T/μ₂₀ — warmer water flows more easily.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the formulas for horizontal and vertical flow.
- Ignoring a thin clay layer (it dominates vertical flow).
- Mixing units of k between layers.

activity.prompt: Two layers 1 m each with k = 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁶ m/s. Vertical equivalent k (×10⁻⁶ m/s, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: For flow parallel to the layers, the equivalent k_h = Σ(k_i H_i)/ΣH_i, a thickness-weighted average dominated by the most permeable layer.
For flow perpendicular to layers (in series), the least permeable layer controls the equivalent k_v.
In stratified soils k_h ≥ k_v, because horizontal flow follows the most permeable layers whereas vertical flow is held back by the least permeable.

quiz.q: k depends on grain size as
quiz.why: Permeability depends on the square of the grain (pore) size, k ∝ D², as in Hazen's and Poiseuille's equations.
A warmer fluid is less viscous, so water flows more easily and k increases with temperature.

lessons.title: Effective stress, seepage pressure and quick sand

scenes.text: Behind a cofferdam, sand suddenly boils up like porridge.
Upward seepage reduced effective stress to zero — quick condition.

steps.title: Effective stress
steps.body:
σ′ = σ − u (Terzaghi). Strength and compressibility depend on σ′.
Saturated soil (no flow) at depth z below water table: σ′ = γ′z.
Upward seepage (gradient i): σ′ = (γ′ − iγ_w)z; downward: (γ′ + iγ_w)z. Seepage force per unit volume j = iγ_w.
Quick condition: σ′ = 0 ⇒ critical gradient i_c = γ′/γ_w = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1. Factor of safety against piping = i_c/i_exit (≥ 3–4 recommended).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Clay γ_sat = 20 kN/m³, water table at surface, depth 5 m: σ = 100, u = 49.05, σ′ = 50.95 kPa.

**Example 2.** Sand G = 2.65, e = 0.65: i_c = 1.65/1.65 = 1.0. Exit gradient 0.25 ⇒ FS = 4.

**Example 3.** Lowering the water table by pumping increases σ′ ⇒ settlement of nearby buildings (a real risk in cities).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total stress for strength calculations.
- Forgetting u = 0 above the water table (ignoring capillarity unless stated).
- Sign of seepage effect (upward reduces σ′).

activity.prompt: Sand: G = 2.68, e = 0.68. Critical hydraulic gradient (2 decimals)?

quiz.why: Terzaghi's effective stress is σ′ = σ − u: total stress minus pore pressure.
Quick condition occurs when upward seepage force cancels the soil's submerged weight, so σ′ = 0 and the soil loses strength.
The critical gradient is i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e), where the effective stress becomes zero.
Downward seepage adds to the soil's weight (seepage force acts down), so effective stress is larger.
Seepage force per unit volume is j = iγ_w.

lessons.title: Flow nets and seepage under structures

scenes.text: Water seeps under a concrete weir from upstream to downstream.
A flow net gives the seepage quantity and the uplift pressures.

steps.title: Flow nets
steps.body:
Flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles forming curvilinear squares (isotropic soil). Seepage q = kH(N_f/N_d) per unit width (N_f flow channels, N_d potential drops, H head loss).
Pore pressure at a point = γ_w × (total head − elevation head). Uplift on structures from equipotentials; exit gradient at the toe = Δh/l (Δh = H/N_d, l = last square size).
Anisotropic soil: transform x by √(k_v/k_h); use k′ = √(k_h k_v).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** H = 6 m, N_f = 4, N_d = 12, k = 10⁻⁵ m/s: q = 10⁻⁵ × 6 × 4/12 = 2×10⁻⁵ m³/s/m = 1.73 m³/day/m.

**Example 2.** Exit square size 1 m: Δh = 0.5 m ⇒ i_exit = 0.5; with i_c = 1 ⇒ FS = 2 (inadequate — add a cut-off or filter).

**Example 3.** Anisotropic k_h = 9×10⁻⁶, k_v = 10⁻⁶: k′ = 3×10⁻⁶ m/s.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting flow lines instead of flow channels.
- Using elevation head as pressure head.
- Ignoring anisotropy in transformed sections.

activity.prompt: Flow net: H = 8 m, N_f = 3, N_d = 12, k = 2×10⁻⁶ m/s. Seepage q (×10⁻⁶ m³/s per m)?

quiz.q: Flow lines and equipotentials meet at
quiz.why: Flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles, which follows from Laplace's equation.
Seepage per unit width is q = k H (N_f/N_d), where N_f is the number of flow channels and N_d the number of potential drops.
The exit gradient is checked against the critical gradient to guard against piping (progressive erosion at the downstream end).
To draw the flow net for anisotropic soil, the section is transformed so that the equivalent permeability is √(k_h k_v).
Total head = elevation head + pressure head (+ velocity head, neglected), so the pressure head is total head − elevation head.

questions.why: Darcy's law is valid only for laminar flow, where velocity is proportional to gradient. It fails in turbulent flow.
Effective stress controls soil strength and volume change (compressibility), which is the basis of soil behaviour.
Clays have very low permeability because their pores are tiny.

questions.q: Falling head k: a 0.5 cm², A 20 cm², L 8 cm, h 60→30 in 300 s
σ′ at 4 m in saturated sand γ_sat 19 (water at surface)
questions.why: With water at the surface, σ′ = 4 × (γ_sat − γ_w) = 4 × (19 − 9.81) = 36.8 kPa.

questions.q: Seepage velocity for v = 10⁻⁴ m/s, n = 0.4
Assertion (A): A thin clay seam drastically reduces vertical permeability of a stratified deposit.  Reason (R): Vertical equivalent k is dominated by the least permeable layer.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: in vertical flow the layers are in series, so the equivalent permeability is controlled by the least permeable layer, and a thin clay seam cuts k_v sharply. The reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: σ′ with upward seepage i = 0.4 at 3 m (γ′ = 10 kN/m³)
FS against piping: i_c 1.05, exit gradient 0.35
Case: A cofferdam flow net has H = 5 m, N_f = 5, N_d = 10, k = 5×10⁻⁵ m/s, wall length 40 m. Daily inflow
Unconfined pumping: q = 0.01 m³/s, r₁ 10 m (h₁ 8 m), r₂ 50 m (h₂ 9 m)
questions.why: For unconfined flow, k = q ln(r₂/r₁)/(π(h₂² − h₁²)) = 0.01 × ln 5/(π × 17) = 0.01 × 1.609/53.4 ≈ 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ m/s.
Hazen: k = C D₁₀² with D₁₀ in cm: 100 × (0.01)² = 0.01 cm/s.

questions.q: Head needed for quick condition in 0.5 m thick sand (i_c 1) with upward flow
questions.why: Quick condition needs i = i_c = 1, and i = h/L, so h = i_c × L = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 m.
For vertical flow, k_v = ΣH/Σ(H/k) = 2/(1/10⁻⁴ + 1/10⁻⁸) = 2/(10⁴ + 10⁸) ≈ 2 × 10⁻⁸ m/s, controlled by the tight layer.

courses.title: Geotechnical Engineering · Unit 3 · Compaction and consolidation
courses.summary: Compaction: Proctor tests, OMC and MDD, zero air voids line, field compaction and control; consolidation: one-dimensional theory, oedometer test, compression and swelling indices, normally and overconsolidated clays, settlement computation, Terzaghi's time factor and coefficient of consolidation.
outcomes: Interpret compaction curves, OMC, MDD and ZAV line
Compute primary consolidation settlement for NC and OC clays
Use time factor to estimate consolidation time
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A highway embankment is built in 300 mm layers compacted by rollers.
The lab Proctor test sets the target density and moisture.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
Compaction = densification by expelling air (not water). Standard Proctor (2.6 kg rammer, 310 mm drop, 3 layers × 25 blows) vs modified Proctor (4.9 kg, 450 mm, 5 layers × 25) — higher energy ⇒ higher MDD, lower OMC.
Dry density ρ_d = ρ/(1 + w). Zero-air-voids line: ρ_d = Gρ_w/(1 + wG) (S = 1); line for air content n_a: ρ_d = (1 − n_a)Gρ_w/(1 + wG).
Dry of optimum: flocculated structure, higher strength, more swelling; wet of optimum: dispersed, more compressible, less permeable (clay cores of dams).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Mould 1000 cm³, wet mass 2.05 kg, w = 15%: ρ = 2.05 g/cc; ρ_d = 1.783 g/cc.

**Example 2.** ZAV at w = 15%, G = 2.7: ρ_d = 2.7/(1 + 0.405) = 1.922 g/cc.

**Example 3.** Relative compaction: field ρ_d 1.75, lab MDD 1.85 ⇒ 94.6% (specs often require ≥ 95% — re-roll).

steps.title: Field compaction
steps.body: Equipment: smooth-wheel rollers (granular base), sheepsfoot (clays), pneumatic-tyred (mixed soils), vibratory rollers/plates (sands). Control: core cutter or sand replacement for field density; nuclear gauges; moisture by rapid methods. Layer thickness and passes trial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking compaction removes water.
- Compacting far wet of optimum (pore pressure, pumping).
- Using wet density instead of dry density for relative compaction.

activity.prompt: Wet density 2.1 g/cc at w = 12%. Dry density (g/cc, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: Compaction densifies soil by mechanical energy, which expels air from the voids (not water).
Modified Proctor uses more compactive energy, so it gives a higher maximum dry density at a lower optimum moisture content.
The zero-air-voids line is ρ_d = Gρ_w/(1 + wG), obtained by putting S = 1.
Sheepsfoot rollers use kneading action, which suits cohesive soils (clays). Clean sands use vibratory rollers.
Relative compaction is the field dry density divided by the laboratory maximum dry density.

scenes.text: The Tower of Pisa leans because the clay beneath one side consolidated more.
Consolidation is slow squeezing of water out of saturated clay under load.

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
Load on saturated clay is first carried by pore water (excess pore pressure), which dissipates as water drains, transferring load to the soil skeleton. Primary consolidation (drainage), secondary compression (creep).
Oedometer: incremental loading, e vs log σ′ plot.

steps.title: Parameters
steps.body:
Coefficient of compressibility a_v = −Δe/Δσ′; m_v = a_v/(1 + e₀) (coefficient of volume change).
Compression index C_c = Δe/Δlog σ′ (virgin line); swelling/recompression index C_r ≈ C_c/5–C_c/10.
Empirical: C_c ≈ 0.009(w_L − 10) (Skempton, undisturbed NC clay).
Preconsolidation pressure σ′_c (Casagrande construction). OCR = σ′_c/σ′₀ (NC: 1; OC > 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using natural log in C_c (it's log₁₀).
- Ignoring preconsolidation (OC clays settle much less).
- Confusing consolidation (time-dependent drainage) with compaction (air expulsion).

activity.prompt: w_L = 60%. Skempton C_c = 0.009(w_L − 10)?

quiz.why: The compression index C_c is the slope of the e–log σ′ line: Δe/Δlog σ′.
Overconsolidation ratio OCR = preconsolidation pressure/present effective stress. For a normally consolidated clay these are equal, so OCR = 1.
Primary consolidation is the gradual squeezing out of pore water under load, which transfers load from pore pressure to the soil skeleton.
The coefficient of volume compressibility is m_v = a_v/(1 + e₀).
Casagrande's graphical construction on the e–log σ′ curve finds the preconsolidation pressure.

scenes.text: A warehouse on a 6 m soft clay layer is expected to settle.
Engineers compute settlement from C_c, e₀ and the stress increase.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
NC clay: S = [C_cH/(1 + e₀)] log₁₀((σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀).
OC clay, σ′₀ + Δσ ≤ σ′_c: S = [C_rH/(1 + e₀)] log((σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀).
OC clay, σ′₀ + Δσ > σ′_c: S = [H/(1 + e₀)][C_r log(σ′_c/σ′₀) + C_c log((σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′_c)].
Alternatively S = m_v Δσ H. Use σ′₀ and Δσ at the mid-depth of the layer (or sub-layers).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** NC clay H = 4 m, e₀ = 1.0, C_c = 0.3, σ′₀ = 60 kPa at mid-depth, Δσ = 40 kPa: S = (0.3 × 4/2) log(100/60) = 0.6 × 0.2218 = 0.133 m.

**Example 2.** Same clay but OC with σ′_c = 120 kPa, C_r = 0.05: S = (0.05 × 4/2) log(100/60) = 0.022 m.

**Example 3.** m_v = 5×10⁻⁴ m²/kN, Δσ = 50 kPa, H = 3 m ⇒ S = 0.075 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using surface stress instead of mid-depth stress.
- Applying C_c to the recompression part.
- Forgetting (1 + e₀) in the denominator.

activity.prompt: NC clay: C_c 0.4, H 3 m, e₀ 1.2, σ′₀ 50 kPa, Δσ 50 kPa. Settlement (m, 3 decimals)?

quiz.why: For normally consolidated clay the settlement is S = [C_c H/(1 + e₀)] log[(σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀], so C_c is used.
Stresses are computed at the mid-depth of the clay layer as an average representative value.
For overconsolidated clay when the final stress stays below the preconsolidation pressure, only the recompression index C_r is used.
Settlement using m_v is S = m_v Δσ H, a linear relation.
Overconsolidated clay is stiffer on the recompression branch, so for the same load it settles less than normally consolidated clay.

Vertical drains shorten the drainage path and speed it up dramatically.

steps.title: Terzaghi's theory
steps.body:
∂u/∂t = c_v ∂²u/∂z². Time factor T_v = c_v t/H_d² (H_d = drainage path: half thickness for double drainage, full thickness for single).
U ≤ 60%: T_v = (π/4)U². U > 60%: T_v = 1.781 − 0.933 log₁₀(100 − U%). T₅₀ = 0.197, T₉₀ = 0.848.
c_v from lab: Casagrande log-time (t₅₀) or Taylor √t (t₉₀). Also c_v = k/(m_v γ_w).
Prefabricated vertical drains and preloading accelerate consolidation (radial drainage).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Clay 6 m, double drainage (H_d = 3 m), c_v = 3 m²/yr: time for 90%: t = 0.848 × 9/3 = 2.54 years.

**Example 2.** Same clay single drainage (H_d = 6 m): t = 0.848 × 36/3 = 10.2 years (4×).

**Example 3.** Lab: 20 mm sample double drained (H_d = 10 mm), t₅₀ = 5 min ⇒ c_v = 0.197 × 100/5 = 3.94 mm²/min.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using full thickness for double drainage.
- Mixing units of c_v (mm²/min vs m²/yr).
- Forgetting time scales with H_d².

quiz.why: t ∝ H_d², so doubling the drainage path makes the time four times longer.
For 90% consolidation the time factor T₉₀ ≈ 0.848.
Vertical drains provide short horizontal drainage paths for pore water, which speeds up consolidation greatly.
The coefficient of consolidation is c_v = k/(m_v γ_w).

Optimum moisture content (OMC) is the water content at which the soil attains maximum dry density for a given compactive effort.

outcomes: Apply τ_f = c′ + σ′ tan φ′ and interpret test results
Compute active and passive pressures and resultants
Outline slope stability factor of safety

scenes.text: After heavy monsoon rain, a hillside road cutting slides.
Rising pore pressure cut the effective stress — and with it the shear strength.

steps.title: Criterion
steps.body:
τ_f = c′ + σ′ tan φ′ (effective stress). Failure plane inclined at θ = 45° + φ′/2 to the major principal plane.
σ₁ = σ₃ tan²(45 + φ/2) + 2c tan(45 + φ/2).
Typical: dense sand φ′ 35–45°, loose sand 28–32°, NC clay c′ ≈ 0, φ′ 20–30°; undrained clay φ_u = 0, strength c_u.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body: Direct shear (box) — simple, fixed failure plane. Triaxial: UU (undrained, quick — short-term stability), CU (with pore pressure measurement ⇒ effective parameters), CD (slow, drained — long-term). Unconfined compression (UCS, σ₃ = 0): c_u = q_u/2. Sensitivity S_t = q_u(undisturbed)/q_u(remoulded). Vane shear in field for soft clays.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** c′ = 10 kPa, φ′ = 30°, σ′ = 100 kPa: τ_f = 10 + 57.7 = 67.7 kPa.

**Example 2.** CD test on sand (c = 0): σ₃ = 100, σ₁ = 300 kPa at failure ⇒ sin φ = (300 − 100)/(300 + 100) = 0.5 ⇒ φ = 30°.

**Example 3.** UCS q_u = 80 kPa ⇒ c_u = 40 kPa; remoulded q_u = 20 ⇒ S_t = 4 (sensitive).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total-stress parameters for long-term drained problems.
- Taking the failure plane angle as 45° − φ/2 from the major principal plane.
- Ignoring pore pressure rise in undrained loading of saturated clay.

activity.prompt: Sand c = 0, φ = 35°, σ′ = 150 kPa. Shear strength (kPa, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: The Mohr–Coulomb failure criterion is τ = c + σ tan φ, where c is cohesion and φ the angle of internal friction.

quiz.q: Failure plane angle with major principal plane
quiz.why: In a soil specimen at failure the failure plane makes an angle 45° + φ/2 with the major principal plane.
In a UCS test σ₃ = 0 and φ = 0, so c_u = q_u/2, where q_u is the unconfined compressive strength.
Long-term stability needs drained conditions (excess pore pressures dissipated), so drained (CD or effective-stress) parameters are used.
With c = 0, sin φ = (σ₁ − σ₃)/(σ₁ + σ₃) = 200/400 = 0.5, so φ = 30°.

scenes.text: A basement wall holds back soil and groundwater.
The soil pushes with active pressure; soil in front resists with passive pressure.

steps.title: Formulas (smooth vertical wall, horizontal backfill)
steps.body:
K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2); K_p = 1/K_a; K₀ ≈ 1 − sin φ′ (at rest).
Active pressure p_a = K_aγz − 2c√K_a; resultant (c = 0) P_a = ½K_aγH² at H/3 from the base.
Surcharge q: uniform K_aq over depth (resultant K_aqH at H/2).
Submerged backfill: use γ′ for soil + full water pressure γ_wz.
Cohesive soil: tension crack depth z_c = 2c/(γ√K_a).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** H = 6 m, γ = 18 kN/m³, φ = 30° (K_a = 1/3): P_a = ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 36 = 108 kN/m at 2 m above base.

**Example 2.** Add surcharge 20 kPa: extra 20/3 × 6 = 40 kN/m at 3 m ⇒ total 148 kN/m.

**Example 3.** Clay c = 15 kPa, φ = 0, γ = 18: z_c = 2 × 15/18 = 1.67 m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using K_p for retained soil.
- Forgetting water pressure behind undrained walls (often doubles the load — provide drainage).
- Taking the resultant at H/2 for triangular pressure.

activity.prompt: φ = 30°, γ = 20 kN/m³, H = 3 m, c = 0. Active thrust P_a (kN/m)?

quiz.why: K_p = 1/K_a = 3 for φ = 30°.

quiz.q: Resultant of triangular active pressure acts at
quiz.why: Active pressure is triangular, and its resultant acts at H/3 above the base (the centroid of the triangle).
Jaky's equation gives the at-rest coefficient K₀ = 1 − sin φ for normally consolidated soil.
Drainage behind a wall reduces water pressure, which is often a large part of the lateral load.

scenes.text: A two-storey house column carries 600 kN to a footing on sandy clay.
Terzaghi's equation gives the ultimate bearing capacity.

steps.title: Terzaghi (general shear)
steps.body:
Strip: q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ (q = γD_f).
Square: 1.3cN_c + qN_q + 0.4γBN_γ; circular: 1.3cN_c + qN_q + 0.3γBN_γ.
φ = 0 (clay): N_c = 5.7, N_q = 1, N_γ = 0 ⇒ q_u = 5.7c + γD_f (Terzaghi); Skempton for clays N_c = 5 (1 + 0.2D/B)(1 + 0.2B/L) ≤ 7.5–9.
Safe bearing capacity q_s = (q_u − γD_f)/FS + γD_f (FS ≈ 3). Water table at base: use γ′ in the 0.5γBN_γ term.
Local shear (loose soils): use c′ = 2c/3, tan φ′ = (2/3)tan φ.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Strip footing B = 2 m, D_f = 1 m, γ = 18, c = 0, φ = 30° (N_q = 22.5, N_γ = 19.7): q_u = 18 × 22.5 + 0.5 × 18 × 2 × 19.7 = 405 + 354.6 = 759.6 kPa; q_s = (759.6 − 18)/3 + 18 = 265 kPa.

**Example 2.** Square footing on clay c_u = 50 kPa, D_f = 1.5 m, γ = 18: q_u = 1.3 × 50 × 5.7 + 27 = 397.5 kPa.

**Example 3.** Column 600 kN, q_s = 200 kPa ⇒ area ≥ 3 m² ⇒ 1.75 m square.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shape factors for strip vs square.
- Not reducing γ for a high water table.
- Ignoring settlement criteria (allowable pressure may be governed by settlement, not shear).

activity.prompt: Clay c_u = 40 kPa, strip footing, D_f = 1 m, γ = 18. Terzaghi q_u = 5.7c + γD_f (kPa)?

quiz.why: Terzaghi's equation for a strip footing is q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ.
For φ = 0 (undrained clay), N_q = e^(π tan φ) tan²(45° + φ/2) = 1 × 1 = 1, while N_γ = 0 and N_c is about 5.14–5.7.
The shape factor for the cohesion term of a square footing is 1.3 (and 0.8 for the γ term).

quiz.q: Water table at the base affects
quiz.why: A water table at the base reduces the unit weight in the N_γ term to the submerged weight γ′.
options: the γ in the N_γ term

quiz.q: Typical factor of safety on bearing capacity
quiz.why: A factor of safety of about 3 is typically applied to the ultimate bearing capacity.

lessons.title: Slope stability and foundation settlement basics

scenes.text: A hill road's embankment must not slip in monsoon.
Factor of safety compares available strength with mobilised stress.

steps.title: Infinite slopes and methods
steps.body:
Dry cohesionless infinite slope: FS = tan φ/tan β (β = slope angle).
With seepage parallel to slope: FS = (γ′/γ_sat)(tan φ/tan β) ≈ ½ the dry value.
Finite slopes: Swedish slip-circle (φ = 0: FS = c_u L_a R/(W x̄)), method of slices (Fellenius, Bishop), Taylor's stability number S_n = c/(F γ H).
Remedies: flatten slope, drainage, retaining structures, soil nailing, vegetation.

steps.title: Foundation settlement (brief)
steps.body: Total settlement = immediate (elastic) + primary consolidation + secondary. Immediate settlement S_i = qB(1 − ν²)I_f/E. Differential settlement causes cracking — limits set by codes (e.g. angular distortion ~1/300–1/500). Plate load and SPT tests are field tools for sands (N-value correlations).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Dry sand φ = 35°, slope β = 25°: FS = 0.700/0.466 = 1.50.

**Example 2.** Same slope with full parallel seepage, γ′/γ_sat = 10/20: FS = 0.75 (unsafe).

**Example 3.** Elastic settlement: q = 150 kPa, B = 2 m, E = 20 MPa, ν = 0.3, I_f = 1: S_i = 150 × 2 × 0.91/20 000 = 13.7 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring pore pressure in wet-season stability checks.
- Using total stress analysis for long-term slopes in clay.
- Confusing allowable bearing pressure (settlement-governed) with safe bearing capacity (shear-governed).

activity.label: Slope angle β for dry sand with φ = 35° (FS = tan φ/tan β)

bands.text: β > φ: FS < 1 — the slope will fail.

quiz.why: For a dry cohesionless infinite slope, FS = tan φ/tan β.

quiz.q: Parallel seepage reduces FS by about
quiz.why: With seepage parallel to the slope, the stabilising effective weight is reduced from γ_sat to γ′, so FS falls to about γ′/γ_sat ≈ half of the dry value.
Bishop's method divides the sliding mass into slices, so it is a method of slices for slope stability.
Total settlement is the sum of immediate (elastic), primary consolidation and secondary compression.
Taylor's stability number is N_s = c/(Fγ H), related to slope angle and depth factor.

Passive pressure is greater than active pressure because K_p > K_a.
Sensitivity is the ratio of undisturbed strength to remoulded strength at the same water content.

questions.why: Soil thrust = ½K_aγH² = ½ × (1/3) × 18 × 25 = 75 kN/m. Surcharge thrust = K_a q H = (1/3) × 10 × 5 = 16.7 kN/m. Total ≈ 91.7 kN/m.

questions.why: Soil thrust uses γ′: ½ × (1/3) × 10 × 16 = 26.7 kN/m. Water thrust = ½ × 9.81 × 16 = 78.5 kN/m. Total ≈ 105.2 kN/m.

questions.q: Case: A square footing 2 m on sand (c = 0, φ = 35°, N_q 41.4, N_γ 42.4), D_f 1 m, γ 18. q_u
questions.why: For a square footing on sand, q_u = qN_q + 0.4γBN_γ = 18 × 41.4 + 0.4 × 18 × 2 × 42.4 = 745 + 611 ≈ 1356 kPa.

questions.why: Safe bearing capacity q_s = (q_u − γD_f)/FS + γD_f = (1356 − 18)/3 + 18 = 446 + 18 ≈ 464 kPa.

courses.title: Transportation · Unit 1 · Highway planning and geometric design
courses.summary: Highway development and road classification in India, highway alignment and surveys, cross-section elements (camber, carriageway, shoulders), sight distances (stopping and overtaking), horizontal alignment (superelevation, radius, extra widening, transition curves) and vertical alignment (gradients, summit and valley curves).
outcomes: Describe road classification and cross-section elements
Compute stopping and overtaking sight distances
Design superelevation, minimum radius and extra widening
Design summit and valley vertical curves
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Highway development, classification and cross-section

scenes.text: A state plans to upgrade a village road to a major district road.
Classification decides design speed, width and cross-section.

steps.title: Classification (Indian practice, nominal)
steps.body:
Non-urban roads: National Highways (NH), State Highways (SH), Major District Roads (MDR), Other District Roads (ODR), Village Roads (VR); expressways for high-speed access-controlled traffic. Urban: arterial, sub-arterial, collector, local streets. Rural roads under national rural road programmes.
Alignment requirements: short, easy, safe, economical; obligatory points; surveys: map study, reconnaissance, preliminary, final location.

steps.title: Cross-section elements
steps.body:
Carriageway width (e.g. 3.5 m per lane for single lane; 7.0 m two-lane); shoulders (≈ 2.5 m); camber/cross slope for drainage (bituminous ≈ 2–2.5%, concrete ≈ 1.5–2%, earth ≈ 3–4%); kerbs; medians; right-of-way and building lines; formation width.
Camber shapes: parabolic, straight-line, combined. Height of crown for straight camber = (W/2)(1/n) for camber 1 in n.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two-lane bituminous road 7.0 m wide with 2.5% camber: crown height = 3.5 × 0.025 = 0.0875 m.

**Example 2.** Camber 1 in 50 on a 7.5 m road: rise = 3.75/50 = 0.075 m.

**Example 3.** Heavy rainfall area, earth road ⇒ steeper camber (≈ 1 in 25–33).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using full width (not half) for crown height.
- Too flat camber on porous surfaces (water ingress).
- Check current IRC codes for values — they are revised periodically.

activity.prompt: Road width 7 m, straight camber 2%. Crown height (m)?

quiz.why: Camber is the cross slope given to a carriageway so that rainwater drains quickly off the surface.
A two-lane carriageway is commonly 7.0 m wide, with each lane 3.5 m.

quiz.q: Earth roads need camber that is
quiz.why: Earth roads are permeable and erode easily, so they need a steeper camber than bituminous or concrete roads to shed water quickly.
The final location survey follows the preliminary survey, where the selected route is marked on the ground.
Expressways and National Highways are the top class of non-urban roads, above MDR, ODR and village roads.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: Sight distances

story.title: Braking for a cow on the road

scenes.text: A driver at 80 km/h sees a cow on the road ahead.
Stopping sight distance = reaction distance + braking distance.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**SSD** = vt + v²/(2gf) (v m/s, t reaction ≈ 2.5 s, f longitudinal friction ≈ 0.35–0.40). On gradient ±n%: braking = v²/(2g(f ± 0.01n)) (+ upgrade). Two-lane two-way roads often need 2 × SSD (intermediate sight distance).
**OSD** = d₁ + d₂ + d₃ = v_b t + (v_b T + 2s) + vT, where s = 0.7v_b + 6 (m), T = √(4s/a), v_b = overtaken vehicle speed (often v − 4.5 m/s), a = acceleration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using km/h in v²/2gf.
- Wrong sign for gradients (downgrade increases braking distance).
- Forgetting that OSD on one-way roads omits d₃.

activity.prompt: SSD for v = 20 m/s, t = 2.5 s, f = 0.4 (g = 9.81), level road (m, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: Stopping sight distance has two parts: lag distance (during reaction time) plus braking distance.
IRC uses a perception–reaction time of 2.5 seconds for stopping sight distance.
On a downgrade the effective friction is reduced to f − 0.01n, so the braking distance is longer.
Overtaking sight distance is d₁ + d₂ + d₃: the distance during the reaction time, the overtaking manoeuvre and the opposing vehicle's travel.
Braking distance = v²/(2gf), so it is proportional to the square of speed.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: Horizontal alignment: superelevation, radius, widening, transitions

scenes.text: Trucks on hill roads need curves that are both banked and wide.
Superelevation, radius and extra widening are designed together.

steps.title: Design relations
steps.body:
Equilibrium: e + f = V²/(127R) (V km/h, R m).
IRC approach: design superelevation for 75% of design speed ignoring friction: e = (0.75V)²/(127R) = V²/(225R); limit e_max (e.g. 7% plains, 10% hills — check current code); if exceeded, check f ≤ 0.15 with e_max.
Ruling minimum radius R = V²/(127(e + f)).
Extra widening W_e = nl²/(2R) (mechanical) + V/(9.5√R) (psychological) (n lanes, l wheelbase ≈ 6 m).
Transition length: rate of change of centripetal acceleration L = 0.0215V³/(CR), C = 80/(75 + V) (0.5–0.8); also by superelevation runoff.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V in m/s in V²/127R (formula uses km/h).
- Exceeding e_max (slow vehicles may slide inwards).
- Forgetting psychological widening.

activity.prompt: V = 60 km/h, R = 150 m. Superelevation by V²/(225R) (3 decimals)?

quiz.why: On a curve e + f = V²/(127R), with V in km/h and R in metres.
IRC designs superelevation for 75% of the design speed, neglecting friction, to suit mixed traffic.
Mechanical widening, to allow for off-tracking, is W_m = nl²/(2R).
Psychological widening is W_ps = V/(9.5√R), allowing for driver tendency to keep clear of the edges.
A transition curve provides a gradual change from straight to circular, so superelevation and centrifugal acceleration build up gradually, which improves comfort.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: Vertical alignment: gradients and vertical curves

scenes.text: Drivers can't see over a crest unless the summit curve is long enough.
Vertical curves are parabolas sized for sight distance.

steps.title: Gradients and curves
steps.body:
Ruling, limiting and exceptional gradients (plain terrain ruling ≈ 3.3%, check code). Grade compensation on curves.
Deviation angle N = |n₁ − n₂| (as fractions).
**Summit curves (SSD):** L > S: L = NS²/4.4 (h₁ = 1.2 m eye, h₂ = 0.15 m object) [general: NS²/(√(2h₁) + √(2h₂))²]; L < S: L = 2S − 4.4/N.
**Valley curves:** comfort (cubic parabola) L = 2√(NV³/C) (V m/s, C ≈ 0.6 m/s³); headlight sight distance (L > S): L = NS²/(1.5 + 0.035S).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Summit: +3% meets −2%: N = 0.05; SSD = 130 m: L = 0.05 × 16 900/4.4 = 192 m (> S ✔).

**Example 2.** Valley: −3% to +2% (N = 0.05), V = 80 km/h (22.22 m/s), C = 0.6: L = 2√(0.05 × 10 974/0.6) = 2√914.5 = 60.5 m; headlight with S = 130: L = 0.05 × 16 900/(1.5 + 4.55) = 139.7 m ⇒ adopt ≈ 140 m.

**Example 3.** Small N = 0.01 with S = 130: L < S case: L = 260 − 440 = negative ⇒ no summit curve needed for sight (use a minimum length for appearance).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using percent instead of fraction for N.
- Choosing the wrong case (L > S or L < S) — check after computing.
- Ignoring the headlight criterion for night driving in valley curves.

activity.prompt: Summit curve: N = 0.06, SSD = 120 m (L > S). Length NS²/4.4 (m, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: The deviation angle N is the algebraic difference of grades: |+2% − (−3%)| = 5% = 0.05.
A summit curve is commonly a simple parabola, which gives a uniform rate of change of grade.
Valley curves are designed for the comfort of passengers (centrifugal effect) and for headlight sight distance at night.

quiz.q: Summit L (L > S) formula with IRC heights
quiz.why: For a summit curve with L > S and IRC eye and object heights (1.2 m and 0.15 m), L = NS²/4.4.
IRC takes the driver's eye height as 1.2 m for sight distance calculations.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

questions.why: Camber helps surface drainage, as it makes water run off to the sides.
IRC uses 2.5 s as the reaction time in stopping sight distance.
Superelevation (banking) provides an inward component of weight to balance the centrifugal force on a curve.

questions.q: Crown height: width 7.5 m, camber 1 in 40

questions.why: N is the algebraic difference of grades: |−2% − 4%| = 6% = 0.06.

questions.q: Assertion (A): IRC designs superelevation for 75% of design speed neglecting friction.  Reason (R): This suits mixed traffic where slow vehicles might slide inward on steep banking.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: IRC designs for 75% of design speed so that slow-moving vehicles on mixed traffic roads do not slide inward on steep banking, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Extra widening: 2 lanes, l 6 m, R 100 m, V 50 km/h
questions.why: Mechanical widening = nl²/(2R) = 2 × 36/200 = 0.36 m; psychological = V/(9.5√R) = 50/95 = 0.53 m. Total ≈ 0.89 m.

questions.q: Case: A 60 km/h road on a 4% downgrade (f 0.37, t 2.5). SSD
questions.why: On a 4% downgrade effective f = 0.37 − 0.04 = 0.33. Lag = 41.7 m, braking = 277.8/(19.62 × 0.33) ≈ 42.9 m, so SSD ≈ 84.6–84.8 m.

questions.q: Valley curve (headlight, L > S): N 0.08, S 90 m
questions.why: For headlight sight distance with L > S: L = NS²/(1.5 + 0.035S) = 0.08 × 8100/(1.5 + 3.15) = 648/4.65 ≈ 139.4 m.

questions.q: Summit curve L < S case: N 0.02, S 150 m
Check: V 100 km/h, R 400 m: e by V²/225R and is e_max 0.07 exceeded?
questions.why: e = V²/(225R) = 10,000/(225 × 400) = 0.111, which exceeds e_max = 0.07. So adopt 0.07 and then check the friction needed.

courses.title: Transportation · Unit 2 · Pavement materials and design
courses.summary: Subgrade soil and CBR, aggregate tests (crushing, abrasion, impact, shape), bitumen tests (penetration, ductility, softening point, viscosity grades), bituminous mix design (Marshall), flexible pavement design concepts (traffic in msa, layered system, IRC approach), and rigid pavement stresses (Westergaard), joints and pavement distress.
outcomes: Interpret subgrade, aggregate and bitumen tests
Compute design traffic in msa and outline flexible design
Compute Westergaard stresses and describe joints and distresses
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Subgrade, aggregates and bitumen

scenes.text: A road built on weak subgrade with soft aggregate develops potholes in one monsoon.
Material tests prevent that.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body:
**Subgrade:** CBR (California Bearing Ratio) = test load/standard load (1370 kg at 2.5 mm; 2055 kg at 5 mm) × 100 — soaked 4 days for design; plate load test (modulus of subgrade reaction k).
**Aggregates:** crushing value (resistance to crushing; lower is better), Los Angeles abrasion (wear), impact value (toughness), flakiness and elongation indices (shape), soundness (weathering), water absorption, stripping value.
**Bitumen:** penetration (hardness, 0.1 mm at 25 °C), ductility, softening point (ring & ball), flash and fire point (safety), viscosity grades (VG-10, VG-30, VG-40 in Indian practice), specific gravity. Modified binders (polymer/crumb rubber) for heavy traffic.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** CBR load at 2.5 mm = 60 kg ⇒ CBR = 60/1370 × 100 = 4.4% (weak subgrade).

**Example 2.** Aggregate crushing: 3 kg sample, 0.75 kg passing 2.36 mm ⇒ ACV = 25%.

**Example 3.** Penetration 60 (0.1 mm units) ⇒ relatively hard binder — suits hotter climates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a higher crushing value means stronger aggregate (it's the reverse).
- Using unsoaked CBR for design in wet regions.
- Overheating bitumen (ageing, fire risk — respect flash point).

activity.prompt: CBR test: load 82.2 kg at 2.5 mm penetration. CBR (%)?

quiz.why: The CBR test compares the load at 2.5 mm penetration with the standard value of 1370 kg (and 2055 kg at 5.0 mm).
A lower aggregate crushing value means less fines are produced under load, so the aggregate is stronger.
The penetration test measures the hardness (consistency) of bitumen, the depth a standard needle sinks in 5 s.
The flash point indicates the temperature at which bitumen vapours ignite, relating to safety during heating.
Indian practice now grades paving bitumen by viscosity (VG-10, VG-30 and so on).

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: Bituminous mix design (Marshall)

scenes.text: A hot-mix plant must produce asphalt that won't rut in summer or crack in winter.
The Marshall method finds the optimum binder content.

steps.title: Marshall parameters
steps.body:
Compacted specimens (e.g. 75 blows per face for heavy traffic) at several binder contents. Measure bulk specific gravity G_mb; theoretical max G_mm; stability (kN, at 60 °C) and flow (mm).
Air voids V_a = (1 − G_mb/G_mm) × 100 (target ≈ 4%); VMA = 100 − G_mb P_s/G_sb; VFB = (VMA − V_a)/VMA × 100.
Optimum binder content (OBC) typically at 4% air voids (check stability, flow, VMA, VFB limits). Mix types: DBM (base), BC (wearing course), SMA, mastic asphalt.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Too much binder (bleeding, rutting) or too little (ravelling, cracking).
- Ignoring VMA minimum (durability).
- Testing at wrong temperature (stability at 60 °C).

activity.prompt: G_mb = 2.35, G_mm = 2.45. Air voids (%, 2 decimals)?

quiz.why: Marshall specimens are tested at 60 °C, which simulates hot pavement in service.
At the optimum binder content, typical design air voids are about 4% for dense mixes.
VFB = (VMA − V_a)/VMA × 100, the percentage of the voids in mineral aggregate filled with binder.
Too much binder fills the voids and squeezes to the surface (bleeding) and the mix becomes soft and rutted.
Wearing courses are commonly bituminous concrete (BC). WMM and GSB are base and sub-base layers.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: Flexible pavement design

scenes.text: A national highway may carry tens of millions of heavy axle loads over its life.
Layer thicknesses are chosen so stresses and strains stay within limits.

steps.title: Design traffic
steps.body:
Cumulative standard axles N (msa) = 365 × A × [(1 + r)ⁿ − 1]/r × D × F / 10⁶, A = initial commercial vehicles/day (after growth to opening), r = growth rate, n = design life, D = lane distribution factor, F = vehicle damage factor (standard axle 80 kN). Fourth-power law: damage ∝ (axle load/standard)⁴.
Layered elastic (mechanistic–empirical) approach in current IRC practice: limit horizontal tensile strain at the bottom of bituminous layer (fatigue cracking) and vertical compressive strain on subgrade (rutting). Typical layers: subgrade → GSB (granular sub-base, drainage) → WMM/base → DBM → BC. Check current IRC:37 edition for catalogues and limits.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A = 2000 CVPD, r = 5%, n = 15 yr, D = 0.75, F = 3.5: growth factor = (1.05¹⁵ − 1)/0.05 = 21.58; N = 365 × 2000 × 21.58 × 0.75 × 3.5/10⁶ ≈ 41.4 msa.

**Example 2.** An overloaded 16 t single axle vs standard 8.16 t: damage ≈ (16/8.16)⁴ ≈ 14.8 standard axles.

**Example 3.** Higher CBR subgrade ⇒ higher modulus (e.g. M_R ≈ 10 × CBR MPa for CBR ≤ 5, per common correlations) ⇒ thinner pavement.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting lane distribution and VDF.
- Using total vehicles instead of commercial vehicles.
- Ignoring overloading (fourth-power damage).

activity.prompt: Axle load 12 t vs standard 8.16 t. Equivalent standard axles by fourth-power law (2 decimals)?

quiz.why: The standard axle load for pavement design is 80 kN (about 8.16 tonnes).
The AASHO road test showed that pavement damage is proportional to the fourth power of axle load.
Mechanistic design of flexible pavements checks fatigue cracking (tensile strain at the bottom of bituminous layer) and rutting (compressive strain on subgrade).
The granular sub-base (GSB) provides drainage and a good working platform, so it supports the upper layers.
msa stands for million standard axles, the unit of design traffic.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: Rigid pavements, joints and distress

scenes.text: Concrete expressways last decades with little maintenance.
Joints control cracking from temperature and shrinkage.

steps.title: Westergaard and stresses
steps.body:
Radius of relative stiffness ℓ = [Eh³/(12(1 − μ²)k)]^(1/4). Wheel load stresses at interior, edge and corner (edge often critical). Corner (Westergaard): σ_c = (3P/h²)[1 − (a√2/ℓ)^0.6].
Temperature (warping) stresses: σ_t = CEαΔt/2 (Bradbury coefficient C). Friction stress from slab contraction.
Joints: contraction (most common, with dowel bars for load transfer), expansion, construction, longitudinal (with tie bars). Dowels transfer load; tie bars hold lanes together.

steps.title: Distresses and maintenance
steps.body: Flexible: fatigue (alligator) cracking, rutting, ravelling, potholes, bleeding, shoving. Rigid: corner cracking, joint spalling, faulting, pumping, scaling. Evaluation: Benkelman beam/FWD deflection, roughness (IRI), skid resistance. Maintenance: crack sealing, surface dressing, overlays, recycling (hot/cold).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Omitting dowel bars at contraction joints on heavy-traffic roads.
- Ignoring combined wheel + temperature stresses.
- Confusing tie bars (no load transfer intent; hold lanes) with dowels (load transfer, allow movement).

activity.prompt: Item → purpose

quiz.q: Radius of relative stiffness depends on
quiz.why: Radius of relative stiffness ℓ = [Eh³/(12(1 − μ²)k)]^(1/4), so it depends on E, h, μ and k.
Dowel bars are placed across transverse (contraction and expansion) joints to transfer load while allowing the slab to move.
Rutting, the permanent wheel-path deformation, is a distress of flexible pavements.
Bradbury's warping stress at the edge is σ_t = C E α Δt/2.
Pumping is the ejection of water and fines from beneath slabs through joints under repeated traffic loads.
options: ejection of fines through joints under traffic

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

questions.why: The California Bearing Ratio test measures the strength of subgrade soil, used in flexible pavement design.
The ductility test measures how far a bitumen briquette can be stretched before breaking.
A rigid pavement uses cement concrete slabs, which distribute loads by slab action.

questions.q: CBR for 2055 kg standard at 5 mm with test load 102.75 kg
Damage of 10.2 t axle vs 8.16 t
questions.why: Using the fourth-power law, damage factor = (10.2/8.16)⁴ = 1.25⁴ ≈ 2.44.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Dowel bars are needed at contraction joints of heavily trafficked concrete pavements.  Reason (R): They transfer wheel loads across the joint while allowing slab movement.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both true: dowel bars carry wheel loads across the joint between slabs (load transfer) while letting the slabs expand and contract, which is why heavily trafficked pavements need them.

questions.q: Warping stress: C 0.8, E 28 000 MPa, α 10⁻⁵, Δt 18 °C
Case: A = 1500 CVPD, r = 7.5%, n = 20 yr, D = 0.75, F = 2.5. Design traffic (msa)
questions.why: The growth factor is (1.075²⁰ − 1)/0.075 ≈ 43.3. Design traffic N = 365 × A × growth factor × D × F/10⁶ = 365 × 1500 × 43.3 × 0.75 × 2.5/10⁶ ≈ 44.4 msa.

questions.q: Aggregate impact value: 350 g sample, 70 g passes 2.36 mm
Radius of relative stiffness ℓ for E 30 000 MPa, h 250 mm, μ 0.15, k 0.08 N/mm³
Overloaded truck axle 18 t: equivalent standard axles
questions.why: By the fourth-power law, equivalent standard axles = (18/8.16)⁴ = 2.206⁴ ≈ 23.7.
The optimum binder content is the binder at the 4% design air voids. The 5.0% sample shows exactly 4.0% voids, so the OBC is 5.0%.

Convert mixed traffic to PCU and estimate capacity
Design signal cycle with Webster's method

lessons.title: Traffic studies and fundamental relations

scenes.text: Every evening, an arterial road slows from 60 km/h to a crawl.
Flow, speed and density explain why maximum flow happens at a moderate speed.

steps.title: Fundamental relation
steps.body:
q = k v_s (flow veh/h = density veh/km × space-mean speed km/h).
Greenshields: v = v_f(1 − k/k_j) ⇒ q = v_f(k − k²/k_j). Maximum flow q_max = v_f k_j/4 at k = k_j/2, v = v_f/2.
Time-mean speed (spot speeds averaged at a point) ≥ space-mean speed (harmonic mean of spot speeds): v_t = v_s + σ²/v_s.
Studies: volume counts (manual, automatic), spot speed (radar, 85th percentile for speed limits), speed and delay (moving observer), origin–destination, parking.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** v_f = 80 km/h, k_j = 120 veh/km: q_max = 80 × 120/4 = 2400 veh/h at k = 60, v = 40 km/h.

**Example 2.** At k = 30: v = 80(1 − 0.25) = 60 km/h; q = 1800 veh/h.

**Example 3.** Spot speeds 40, 50, 60 km/h: time-mean = 50; space-mean = 3/(1/40 + 1/50 + 1/60) = 48.6 km/h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using time-mean speed in q = kv (use space-mean).
- Assuming highest speed gives highest flow.
- Mixing units (veh/km with m/s).

activity.prompt: Greenshields: v_f = 60 km/h, k_j = 150 veh/km. Maximum flow (veh/h)?

quiz.why: Traffic flow equals density times space-mean speed: q = k·v, in veh/h = (veh/km) × (km/h).

quiz.q: Max flow in Greenshields at density
quiz.why: In Greenshields' linear model q = v_f k(1 − k/k_j) is a parabola, whose peak is at k = k_j/2.
With v = v_f(1 − k/k_j), at k = k_j/2 (capacity) the speed is v_f/2.
Speed limits are commonly fixed at the 85th percentile spot speed, a speed which 85% of drivers do not exceed.
Space-mean speed is the harmonic mean of spot speeds. It is the average over a stretch of road, weighting slow vehicles properly.

sources: IRC guidelines (topic reference; check current editions)

lessons.title: PCU, capacity and level of service

scenes.text: Indian roads mix cars, trucks, buses, two-wheelers and auto-rickshaws.
Passenger car units put them on a common scale.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
PCU (passenger car unit) converts vehicle types to car equivalents (values depend on speed, road width and composition — use the current IRC/Indo-HCM tables). Typical illustrative values: car 1.0, two-wheeler ~0.5 or less, auto-rickshaw ~1.0–1.2, bus/truck ~3–4, cycle ~0.5, animal cart ~6–8.
Capacity: maximum hourly flow under prevailing conditions; basic (ideal) vs possible vs practical capacity. Theoretical lane capacity C = 1000V/S (S = average spacing in m, V km/h); S = vt + L (headway approach).
Level of service (LOS A–F) by volume/capacity ratio, density or speed.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Counts per hour: 400 cars (1.0), 600 two-wheelers (0.5), 100 buses (3.0), 200 autos (1.2) ⇒ 400 + 300 + 300 + 240 = 1240 PCU/h.

**Example 2.** V = 60 km/h (16.67 m/s), reaction 0.75 s for spacing, vehicle length 6 m: S = 16.67 × 0.75 + 6 = 18.5 m ⇒ C = 1000 × 60/18.5 = 3243 veh/h (theoretical upper bound).

**Example 3.** Road capacity 1800 PCU/h, flow 1240 ⇒ V/C = 0.69.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a single fixed PCU set for all conditions.
- Confusing capacity with design service volume.
- Treating theoretical C = 1000V/S as practical capacity.

lessons.title: Intersections and signal design

scenes.text: A city junction jams at peak hours with a fixed 2-minute signal.
Webster's method finds an optimum cycle length.

steps.title: Webster's method
steps.body:
Critical flow ratio per phase y = q/s (s = saturation flow). Y = Σy (critical).
Total lost time L = Σ(start-up loss + clearance) per phase (e.g. 2–4 s per phase) + all-red.
Optimum cycle C₀ = (1.5L + 5)/(1 − Y). Effective green split: g_i = (y_i/Y)(C₀ − L).
Saturation flow (illustrative): s ≈ 525W PCU/h for approach width W (m) (common old approximation; use current guidance).

steps.title: Intersection types
steps.body: At-grade: uncontrolled, priority (stop/give-way), channelised, rotaries/roundabouts (weaving; suitable for moderate volumes), signalised. Grade-separated: interchanges (cloverleaf, diamond, trumpet) for high volumes. Pedestrian facilities: zebra crossings, refuge islands, foot over-bridges, subways.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two phases: N–S q = 600, s = 1800 (y = 0.333); E–W q = 450, s = 1500 (y = 0.3); Y = 0.633; L = 10 s: C₀ = (15 + 5)/0.367 = 54.5 ≈ 55 s. Effective greens: (0.333/0.633)(45) = 23.7 s, (0.3/0.633)(45) = 21.3 s.

**Example 2.** If Y ≥ 1 the junction cannot be served by signals alone ⇒ widen, add lanes or grade-separate.

**Example 3.** Saturation flow for a 7 m approach ≈ 525 × 7 = 3675 PCU/h (rough).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total flow instead of the critical lane/approach flow.
- Forgetting lost time.
- Very long cycles increase delay — not always better.

As Y → 1 the junction is close to saturation, so (1 − Y) → 0 and the optimum cycle becomes very large.

The 4 Es: Engineering (geometry, signs, markings, lighting, crash barriers, speed calming), Enforcement, Education, Emergency care. Road safety audits at design, construction and pre-opening stages.

lessons.title: Permanent way and gauges

scenes.text: Most Indian main lines are broad gauge — 1676 mm between rails.
Rails, sleepers, ballast and fastenings together form the permanent way.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
**Gauges:** broad gauge 1676 mm (Indian main lines), standard gauge 1435 mm (metros and high-speed lines in India use it too), metre gauge 1000 mm, narrow 762/610 mm. Uni-gauge policy converts MG to BG.
**Rails:** flat-footed (e.g. 52 kg, 60 kg/m), long welded rails reduce joints. Functions: guide wheels, transfer load.
**Sleepers:** concrete (PSC, most common now), wooden, steel; sleeper density e.g. M + 7 (number per rail length).
**Ballast:** crushed stone; drains water, distributes load, holds sleepers; depth ≈ 250–350 mm under sleeper.
**Fastenings:** elastic rail clips, liners, rubber pads. **Coning of wheels** (1 in 20) keeps the train centred and helps on curves; **creep** = longitudinal movement of rails.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Sleeper density M + 7 with 13 m rails (M = 13): 20 sleepers per rail length.

**Example 2.** Rail weight 60 kg/m ⇒ a 13 m rail weighs 780 kg.

**Example 3.** Wheel coning ensures that on curves the outer wheel runs on a larger diameter, reducing slip.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing gauge with the distance between wheel flanges.
- Thinking ballast is only a cushion (drainage is key).
- Ignoring creep anchors on long rails.

lessons.title: Railway curves, cant and speeds

scenes.text: On curves the outer rail is raised so passengers don't feel thrown outward.
Cant balances the centrifugal force at the equilibrium speed.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
Equilibrium cant e = GV²/(127R) (G = gauge centre-to-centre of rails in mm ≈ 1750 mm for BG; V km/h; R m; e in mm).
Cant deficiency = cant required for maximum speed − actual cant (limits e.g. 75 mm BG, check rules).
Degree of curve D: R = 1750/D (for 30.5 m chord, BG convention) — depends on chord length used.
Transition length and safe speed checks; grade compensation on curves (e.g. 0.04% per degree for BG).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** BG, G = 1750 mm, R = 800 m, equilibrium speed 80 km/h: e = 1750 × 6400/(127 × 800) = 110.2 mm.

**Example 2.** Max speed 110 km/h on the same curve: required cant = 1750 × 12 100/(101 600) = 208.4 mm; with 110 mm provided ⇒ deficiency 98 mm (exceeds 75 mm ⇒ reduce speed or increase cant within limits).

**Example 3.** Speed allowed with 110 mm cant + 75 mm deficiency: V = √(185 × 127 × 800/1750) = 103 km/h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using rail gauge 1676 instead of centre-to-centre ≈ 1750 mm in the cant formula.
- Ignoring cant excess for slow freight trains.
- Units (V km/h, R m, e mm).

lessons.title: Train resistance and hauling capacity

scenes.text: A locomotive must haul a 4000 t coal train up a gradient.
Resistances from friction, gradient and curves set the maximum load.

steps.title: Resistances
steps.body:
- Rolling and journal friction, wave action, wind and speed-dependent resistance — often lumped: R = (0.0016 + 0.00008V + 0.0000006V²) W (illustrative empirical form; W in tonnes ⇒ R in tonnes).
- **Gradient resistance:** W × (gradient) (e.g. 1 in 200 ⇒ W/200).
- **Curve resistance** (BG approx.): 0.0004 W D (D = degree of curve).
- Starting resistance higher.
Hauling capacity = μ × weight on driving wheels (adhesion, μ ≈ 0.2–0.3). Train load capacity found by equating tractive effort to total resistance.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Gradient resistance of a 3000 t train on 1 in 150: 20 t (≈ 196 kN).

**Example 2.** Curve 2° on BG: 0.0004 × 3000 × 2 = 2.4 t.

**Example 3.** Loco with 120 t on driving axles, μ = 0.25 ⇒ hauling capacity 30 t (≈ 294 kN) of tractive force — the total resistance of the train on the ruling gradient must be below this.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting gradient resistance dominates on steep sections.
- Using total loco weight instead of weight on driving wheels for adhesion.
- Unit mix-ups (tonnes-force vs kN).

Hauling capacity is limited by adhesion: coefficient of adhesion × weight on the driving wheels.
For BG, curve resistance is approximated as 0.0004 W D, with D the degree of curve.
The ruling gradient is the steepest gradient that governs the maximum load a locomotive can haul over the section.
The adhesion between steel wheel and steel rail is low, about 0.2 to 0.3.

scenes.text: A state plans a regional airport for turboprop aircraft.

steps.title: Runway orientation and length
steps.body:
**Wind rose:** runway oriented along prevailing winds so that crosswind components stay within limits; wind coverage ≥ 95% is a common target (ICAO).
**Basic runway length** (standard conditions: sea level, 15 °C, zero gradient, no wind) corrected for:
- Elevation: +7% per 300 m above MSL.
- Temperature: +1% per 1 °C of airport reference temperature above standard atmosphere at that elevation (T_std = 15 − 0.0065h).
- Total correction for elevation + temperature should not exceed 35% (else special study).
- Gradient: +20% per 1% of effective gradient (after above corrections).
Airport components: runways, taxiways, aprons, terminal, control tower, hangars; obstruction clearance surfaces; markings and lighting.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Basic length 1800 m, elevation 300 m ⇒ +7% ⇒ 1926 m.
Airport reference temperature 30 °C; standard at 300 m = 15 − 1.95 = 13.05 °C ⇒ rise 16.95 ⇒ +16.95% ⇒ 1926 × 1.1695 = 2252 m (total correction 25% < 35% ✔).
Effective gradient 0.5% ⇒ +10% ⇒ 2478 m.

**Example 2.** Crosswind component = V sin θ: wind 30 km/h at 30° to the runway ⇒ 15 km/h.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying corrections to the basic length instead of sequentially.
- Forgetting the 35% check.
- Orienting runways by the strongest wind only (coverage over the year matters).

The senior engineer explains that the beam is designed so that steel yields first and the beam warns by cracking and deflecting before it fails.

steps.title: Limit states and partial factors
steps.body: Design checks **limit states of collapse** (flexure, shear, torsion, compression) and **serviceability** (deflection, cracking). Loads are multiplied by a factor, typically **1.5 (DL+LL)**. Material strengths are divided by partial factors: **γc = 1.5** for concrete and **γs = 1.15** for steel, so design steel stress = fy/1.15 = **0.87 fy**.

steps.title: Assumptions and the stress block
steps.body:
- Plane sections remain plane.
- Maximum compressive strain in concrete at the extreme fibre in bending = **0.0035**.
- Tensile strength of concrete is ignored.
- Rectangular equivalent block: compressive force C = **0.36 fck b xu**, acting at **0.42 xu** from the top fibre.
- Steel design stress is 0.87 fy at yield.

steps.title: Balanced limit
steps.body: The neutral axis depth is limited so that steel strain is at least yield strain + 0.002. This gives **xu,max/d = 0.53 (Fe250), 0.48 (Fe415), 0.46 (Fe500)**. Beams are designed as **under-reinforced** (xu < xu,max) because failure is ductile. For Fe415, **Mu,lim = 0.138 fck b d²**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using fy instead of 0.87 fy in the strength formulas.
- Forgetting that the moment from factored loads is Mu, not the service moment.
- Mixing N·mm and kN·m: divide N·mm by 10⁶ to get kN·m.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body:
1. Ast = number of bars × π/4 × φ².
2. xu = 0.87 fy Ast / (0.36 fck b).
3. Compare with xu,max = k·d (k = 0.46 for Fe500).
4. If xu ≤ xu,max, Mu = 0.87 fy Ast (d − 0.42 xu). Otherwise Mu = Mu,lim.

- Taking d as overall depth D. Effective depth d = D − cover − stirrup − φ/2 (500 − 30 − 8 − 10 = 452, drawings often round to 450).

lessons.title: Shear in RC beams: tau_v and tau_c

scenes.text: During inspection of a 20-year-old warehouse, an engineer finds inclined cracks at about 45 degrees near the support of a beam.
There is almost no flexural cracking at mid-span. The cause is shear, not bending.

steps.title: Nominal shear stress
steps.body: τv = Vu / (b d). Concrete alone resists τc, which depends on the percentage of tension steel pt = 100 Ast/(b d) and grade (IS 456 Table 19). The maximum permitted τc,max is **2.8 (M20), 3.1 (M25), 3.5 (M30)** N/mm²; if τv exceeds it, the section size must be increased.

steps.title: Stirrups
steps.body: If τv > τc the stirrups carry Vus = Vu − τc b d. For vertical stirrups: **Vus = 0.87 fy Asv d / sv**. Even when τv < τc, minimum shear reinforcement is required: **Asv / (b sv) ≥ 0.4 / (0.87 fy)**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Beam 250 × 500, d = 450, support shear Vu = 90 kN: τv = 90,000 / (250 × 450) = **0.80 N/mm²**. For pt = 0.84% in M25, τc ≈ 0.59 N/mm². τv > τc so design stirrups for Vus = 90,000 − 0.6 × 112,500 ≈ 22.5 kN (using τc = 0.6).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Vu at the face of support instead of at distance d from the face (for the usual case).
- Forgetting minimum shear reinforcement and max spacing: lesser of **0.75 d or 300 mm**.

story.title: A column that looked too thin

scenes.text: On a retail building project, the architect wants 300 mm square columns in place of 400 mm. You must explain what the code needs.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Short vs slender
steps.body: A column is short if le/D < 12 (both directions). Slender columns need additional moments. Minimum eccentricity: **emin = l/500 + D/30 ≥ 20 mm**. If emin ≤ 0.05 D, the axial formula can be used.

steps.title: Axial capacity
steps.body: **Pu = 0.4 fck Ac + 0.67 fy Asc**, where Ac = Ag − Asc.

steps.title: Detailing
steps.body:
- Longitudinal steel: minimum 0.8%, maximum 6% of gross area (4% is used at laps in practice).
- Min bars: 4 in a rectangular column, 6 in a circular column.
- Ties: diameter at least one quarter of the largest bar and not less than 6 mm; spacing least of least lateral dimension, 16 × smallest longitudinal bar diameter, 300 mm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Ag instead of Ac in the concrete term.
- Spacing ties at 300 mm in all cases without checking 16φ.
